title: From Rescue Teams To Relief Funds, How Nepal Is Responding To Flood Crisis - NDTV
description: From Rescue Teams To Relief Funds, How Nepal Is Responding To Flood Crisis  NDTV
publisher.title: NDTV
full_article:
Nepal's search and rescue operation was still underway, when the country was hit by an earthquake on September 8. The casualties from the glacier outburst, that took place on August 26, is increasing every day. The latest government update puts the death count at 1,367, with more than 5,100 people missing. So far, 13,646 people have been rescued, while 7,151 are receiving treatment. More than 21,000 security personnel have been deployed for the response.

The floods followed a collapse in the Himalayan region that sent a large volume of water, mud and debris into the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river corridors.

Countries Step In

Nepal has received help from several countries as its own rescue teams continue to work across the affected areas. India, China and South Korea have provided specialised rescue and forensic support, while countries including the UAE, Japan, Australia, Singapore, Malaysia, the UK and US have sent money, relief material, equipment or technical assistance.

India has sent about 95 tonnes of relief material and 54 personnel, including tunnel-rescue experts, forensic specialists and medical personnel. Indian teams are also helping Nepal with DNA identification and tunnel rescue.

China has sent rescue equipment and supplies, including drones and equipment for DNA identification. South Korea has also provided a rescue team and forensic assistance. These teams are working alongside Nepalese authorities as the search continues.

Relief Fund Builds Up

Alongside the physical relief effort, donations have been flowing into Nepal's Prime Minister's Disaster Relief Fund. The fund had nearly Nepalese rupee 12 billion available as of September 8, according to the Ministry of Finance, Nepal.

Of this, NPR 8.77 billion was in local currency and NPR 3.18 billion equivalent in dollar accounts.

The government reported NPR 9.87 billion was collected since the floods, while NPR 2.08 billion was already available before the disaster.

The government has also transferred NPR 1 billion to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority for the response.

title: China’s Aid to Nepal: A New Model of Global South Cooperation? - Modern Diplomacy
description: China’s Aid to Nepal: A New Model of Global South Cooperation?  Modern Diplomacy
publisher.title: Modern Diplomacy
full_article:
China’s aid model to Nepal, especially during crises and natural disasters, is a prime example of Global South solidarity, presented by Beijing as a development alternative to Western aid that is often contingent on political and structural reforms. This partnership primarily aims to serve the objectives of China’s Belt and Road Initiative by transforming Nepal from a landlocked country into a land-connected one through infrastructure networks traversing the Himalayas. In this respect, China’s aid model to Nepal exemplifies Beijing’s strategy of strengthening solidarity with countries of the Global South. These relations transcend traditional relief efforts, encompassing strategic and economic partnerships through which China seeks to offer a development alternative to conditional Western aid. For instance, China sent emergency humanitarian aid packages, cash assistance, and a team of experts to Nepal to assist those affected by the devastating mudslides and floods that struck the border region between the two countries in late August 2026. Chinese humanitarian aid to Nepal arrived in several phases. Successive shipments of supplies, including tents, blankets, sleeping bags, dry biscuits, and emergency necessities, were transported to Kathmandu via special Chinese transport aircraft. China also dispatched numerous specialized relief teams, tunnel rescue experts, and DNA experts to assist in search and identification operations. China provided extensive logistical and informational support to Nepal. It shared satellite data, aerial photographs, and hydrological data with Nepal and provided direct assistance to 1,720 Nepalese residents stranded in the Gyirong border district.

This Chinese model of solidarity with Nepal is part of Beijing’s efforts to strengthen its relations with developing countries and provide humanitarian relief and technological support in shared border regions. These Chinese relief, development, and humanitarian initiatives contribute to crisis response in developing countries like Nepal, mitigating the effects of natural disasters through the exchange of hydrological data and satellite imagery for monitoring floods and landslides and providing direct logistical and humanitarian support to populations trapped in rugged areas, such as the border region of Gyirong. This strengthens the strategic depth of Sino-Nepalese relations within the framework of China’s Belt and Road Initiative. This Chinese model of solidarity with developing countries can be analyzed through several geopolitical and economic dimensions, including China’s presentation of solidarity with the Global South and its development alternative. China’s aid to Nepal is based on the principles of South-South Cooperation, which differ from the Western model in characteristics such as non-interference in the internal affairs of states. This contrasts with Western aid and projects, such as the US Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC) program.

The MCC program sparked political debate in Nepal. Furthermore, while China does not impose conditions related to governance or economic privatization, the West imposes political and economic conditions. Chinese aid is characterized by its flexibility in humanitarian crises. This Chinese solidarity was evident in its immediate response to natural disasters, such as the recent floods and mudslides in Nepal in August and September 2026. Beijing promptly sent emergency relief packages, provided cash assistance, deployed tunnel rescue experts, and shared satellite and hydrological data free of charge. This aligns with China’s Belt and Road Initiative, in which Nepal has been a strategic partner since the signing of a memorandum of understanding in 2017, culminating in the signing of a joint executive framework for cooperation. Furthermore, China is assisting Nepal in building the Nepal-Himalayan Connectivity Network, a multi-dimensional transportation and communications network encompassing roads and railways, such as the trans-Tibet-Kathmandu railway. Chinese aid and investment also extend to energy security, hydropower, and international airports, such as Pokhara International Airport, to facilitate trade and tourism.

This Chinese model of solidarity with Nepal and the Global South can be analyzed through several key axes that reflect the features of Chinese solidarity with the Global South, through (China’s focus on infrastructure and continental connectivity). Chinese investment aid in Nepal has been primarily concentrated on the infrastructure and transportation sector, the most prominent feature of China’s Belt and Road Initiative, which Nepal joined in 2017. The Chinese presence in Nepalese transportation projects also played a significant role in China’s rapid identification of all the gaps after the landslide crisis, especially with the participation of Chinese companies in the Trans-Himalayan Railway project linking Lhasa (Tibet) to the Nepalese capital, Kathmandu. In addition, China has financed international airport models for countries in the Global South, including Nepal. China has financed and built vital projects, such as Pokhara International Airport. China has also participated in building hydroelectric power plants to help Nepal achieve energy self-sufficiency and export surplus energy.

Thus, China’s model of solidarity, humanitarian aid, and crisis response in Nepal served as a clear example of unconditional Chinese solidarity with the Global South. China promotes its aid model as being based on respect for sovereignty and non-interference in internal affairs, a principle widely accepted in the Global South. This was not the first instance of Chinese aid to Nepal; it had previously provided emergency humanitarian assistance during the 2015 earthquake, delivering financial aid packages and deploying large rescue teams to help rebuild Nepal after the devastating quake. The same pattern repeated itself after the COVID-19 pandemic, with Beijing being among the first suppliers of vaccines and medical supplies to Nepal at a time when the Global South was grappling with vaccine nationalism in the West.

Thus, Chinese humanitarian aid in response to crises in the Global South aimed to (reduce economic dependence on the West and provide alternatives). Historically, Nepal, a landlocked country, relied almost entirely on India for trade and access to seaports. However, China signed transit agreements and protocols with Nepal, granting it access to Chinese sea and land ports. This broke the historical geographic monopoly and provided Nepal with strategic alternatives to enhance its national and economic security. Chinese solidarity with Nepal also included support for sustainable development projects and technical assistance. Chinese aid encompassed technology transfer and local capacity building in agriculture, education, and healthcare through scholarships for Nepalese students and training for technical personnel. Comparing the Chinese aid model with the Western model in the Global South, using Nepal as a case study, reveals the following :

Points of Comparison The Chinese Model (Applied in Nepal) The Traditional Western Model Preconditions and the Nature of Conditionality Unconditional politically, focusing on mutual benefit, respect for sovereignty, and non-interference in internal affairs Conditional on transparency, human rights, and structural reform, as well as conditions related to political reforms, human rights, and economic restructuring Area of focus and sectoral focus Hard infrastructure (roads, bridges, energy, airports, and emergency relief) Governance, education, humanitarian relief, civil society, institution building, and health Speed and execution High speed in decision-making and project initiation Bureaucratic procedures and lengthy evaluations before funding Financing Mechanism A mix of grants, concessional loans, and interest-free loans Focuses on development grants or loans from international financing agencies

By understanding the preceding table, we can grasp the comparisons between the Chinese model (as applied in Nepal and other countries of the Global South) and the traditional Western model. In terms of preconditions, the Chinese aid model is politically unconditional, focusing on mutual benefit. The Chinese model of solidarity with the Global South and Nepal is based on the principle of respecting sovereignty and non-interference in internal affairs. In contrast, the Western aid model is conditional on transparency, human rights, and structural reform, as well as conditions related to political reforms, human rights, and economic restructuring. Regarding the focus and sectors, Chinese humanitarian and development aid prioritizes hard infrastructure (roads, bridges, energy, airports, and humanitarian relief), while the traditional Western model focuses on governance, education, humanitarian relief, civil society, institution building, and health. Finally, concerning the speed and procedures in humanitarian and development aid and crisis response in the Global South, the Chinese side is characterized by rapid decision-making and project initiation, while the Western model is criticized for its slow pace. The West relies on bureaucratic procedures and lengthy evaluations before providing funding. In contrast, the Chinese model of solidarity financing is based on a mix of grants, concessional loans, and interest-free loans, while Western financing focuses primarily on development grants or loans from international financial institutions.

Finally,spite the pragmatism of the Chinese model of solidarity with developing countries, there are numerous practical challenges and complexities. Although this model is presented as a solidarity-based alternative, it is not without its challenges on the ground, particularly in Nepal, where the balance between loans and grants is a key issue. There has been ongoing political debate within Nepal urging Beijing to provide grants instead of concessional loans to avoid debt burdens and a recurrence of financial default scenarios. Furthermore, there is geopolitical caution, as Nepal finds itself navigating a delicate balancing act between the influence of its northern neighbor (China) and its deep historical and economic ties with India and the United States, creating numerous complications and challenges for the country.

title: Nepal: Call to solidarity with education communities following devastating floods and landslides - Education International
description: Nepal: Call to solidarity with education communities following devastating floods and landslides  Education International
publisher.title: Education International
full_article:
Education International (EI) has launched a call for solidarity to support its affiliates in Nepal as they assist teachers and students affected by devastating floods and landslides that caused widespread destruction in the districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Gorkha, and Dhading on 26 August.

The catastrophic flash floods swept away everything in their path – homes, schools, bridges, and other infrastructure – devastating entire communities. Tens of thousands of people have been affected, with more than 1,200 people having lost their lives and thousands of others still missing.

Education International, which represents four member organisations in Nepal – the Nepal Teachers' Association (NTA), the Nepal National Teachers' Association (NNTA), the Nepal School Employees Council (NSEC), and the Institutional Schools Teachers Union (ISTU) – expressed its deepest sympathy and solidarity with all teachers, students, education support personnel, and communities affected.

Reacting to the tragedy, EI General Secretary David Edwards declared: “Our heartfelt solidarity is with all those facing loss, uncertainty, and displacement, including families grieving loved ones and those whose homes, schools, and livelihoods have been destroyed or severely affected.”

The education sector has been particularly affected by the disaster: numerous schools have been destroyed or rendered unusable, leaving thousands of students and teachers without access to classes. Accounts have also begun to emerge of education staff acting swiftly to protect students, helping to save many lives.

The NNTA and the NTA have reached out to EI to request support and assistance for the affected teachers, students, and school communities. The unions reported that at least 22 teachers and more than 300 students are currently missing or deceased. At least 18 schools have been completely destroyed, and dozens of other establishments suffered partial damage. More than 19,000 students have been directly affected by the disaster, many of whom have lost their parents, homes, and schools.

The figures are appalling, but NNTA President Hansha Bahadur Shahi warns that the reality is very likely much worse: “The situation on the ground is more serious than the preliminary figures indicate. Entire settlements have been swept away, and many affected areas remain difficult to access. There are also continuing fears of further flooding. We are still collecting and verifying information to establish the full extent of the damage and loss of life.”

“Thousands of students have been deprived of their fundamental right to education”, reported Soma Nath Giri, NTA President. “With school buildings, teaching and learning materials, and educational infrastructure destroyed, there is an urgent and growing demand for emergency assistance from the affected districts.”

Students search for their belongings at Shree Bageshwori Secondary School in Baireni, Dhading district, Nepal, on August 31, 2026. (Photo credit: Subaas Shrestha/NurPhoto)

At a time when schools should provide stability, safety, and hope, many students, teachers, and education support personnel are now confronting immense challenges. “During this difficult time, we pay tribute to the teachers, education support personnel, first responders, volunteers, and local communities who are working tirelessly to provide assistance and support to those in need,” stated Anand Singh, EIAP regional director. “Their commitment and compassion are a powerful reminder that resilience grows through solidarity, care, and collective action.”

The two union presidents, Hansa Bahadur Shahi and Soma Nath Giri, identified the most urgent needs for the teacher unions: “The immediate priorities are to ensure the safety and protection of school-age children, establish temporary learning facilities, and provide psychosocial support to children, teachers, and affected families. Education must be restored as soon as possible, alongside relief, protection, and recovery efforts.”

No education community should have to face such devastation alone. The strength of the global education union movement lies in its solidarity, transforming concern into meaningful support that helps communities meet urgent needs, restore access to education, rebuild schools, and renew hope. As affected communities begin the challenging process of recovery and reconstruction, Education International reaffirms its unwavering commitment to standing with every education worker impacted by this disaster and to safeguarding the right to education for all learners.

title: Two weeks after Himalayan flood, Nepal searches while Tibet rebuilds - EFE - Agencia de noticias
description: Two weeks after Himalayan flood, Nepal searches while Tibet rebuilds  EFE - Agencia de noticias
publisher.title: EFE - Agencia de noticias
full_article:
Kathmandu/Beijing, Sep 9 (EFE).- Two weeks after a surge of ice, water, and rocks swept through the Himalayas, Nepal is still searching for thousands of missing people, while neighboring Tibet has restored key infrastructure and begun returning evacuees home.

The disaster has left sharply different recovery scenarios on either side of the border, with Nepal still struggling to locate and identify victims while Tibet moves toward recovery.

Thousands missing in Nepal

Nepal has recovered 1,367 bodies and lists 5,133 people as missing, including 587 foreign tourists, compared with 43 deaths and 519 missing people reported by Chinese authorities in Tibet.

Of those missing in Tibet, 261 are foreigners from 23 countries.

More than 21,000 personnel are taking part in rescue and recovery operations in Nepal.

Some searches are focused on hydroelectric power plants where large numbers of workers were trapped, although authorities have yet to establish how many people remain underground.

The most recent survivors were rescued on Sep. 4 and 5, when four people were pulled alive from the facilities.

In Tibet, more than 2,500 rescuers and hundreds of vehicles have been deployed around Gyirong.

Operations were initially hampered by the destruction of the area’s only land route, power, and communications outages, and the risk of a new flood caused by a natural dam upstream.

Glacier collapse identified as likely trigger

Initial analyses indicate that the disaster began with the collapse of a high-altitude glacier in Nepalese territory, an explanation accepted by China and later supported by international satellite analyses.

Chinese experts have placed the fracture at an altitude of between 5,200 and 5,400 meters and described a chain reaction in which falling ice swept up rocks and debris, creating a mudflow that reached Gyirong, Tibet, in about seven minutes.

Chinese specialists have ruled out the possibility that the disaster was caused by the bursting of a glacial lake.

Nepal initially said the cause had not been fully established as investigations into the origin of the avalanche continued.

Recovery, return move at different speeds

In Nepal, the destruction has left communities in Rasuwa and Nuwakot facing severe access problems.

The Red Cross and Red Crescent have warned that some families remain without essential services and estimated that journeys that previously took about three hours can now require nine hours or more.

Nepal began reopening schools in Bidur on Wednesday after a two-week closure.

In Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading, 23 educational centers have been affected, with more than 7,000 students enrolled. About 600 children remain missing.

In Tibet, the land route to Gyirong was restored a week after the disaster, allowing heavy machinery to enter the area and communications to be progressively restored.

Of the 499 residents evacuated from five villages, 444, almost nine in 10, have already returned home.

Nepal struggles to identify victims

Nepal had returned just 102 of the 1,367 recovered bodies and remains to families by Wednesday, fewer than one in 10.

Police have collected 2,698 DNA samples, 1,286 from human remains and 1,412 from relatives, including samples taken abroad to help identify foreign tourists.

A lack of space in morgues has also forced authorities to temporarily bury unidentified victims.

In Gyirong, China has deployed laboratories and forensic teams to identify recovered bodies through DNA testing and other forensic procedures.

Access to the aftermath

In Nepal, national and international journalists have worked on the ground since the early days of the disaster, gaining access to affected communities, hospitals, morgues, and cemeteries and speaking directly with survivors and relatives.

Authorities have issued frequent updates, although figures have sometimes differed between agencies as lists of dead and missing have been revised.

In Tibet, information about casualties, rescue operations, and damage came primarily from government authorities and state media during the first days after the disaster.

Beijing also suspended the issuance of permits for border areas under special control in Shigatse, including Gyirong, citing the risk of further disasters.

A small group of foreign journalists was allowed into Gyirong on Sep. 5 and 6, 10 days after the flood, on a visit organized by Chinese authorities.

China’s latest official death toll, released Sunday, had not been updated by Wednesday.

Human Rights Watch has accused Beijing of “censorship and control” of information and criticized what it described as the limited presence of victims’ voices in the public account of the disaster. EFE

description: Nepal flooding kills 1,300, hundreds still missing  FOX 9 Minneapolis-St. Paul
publisher.title: FOX 9 Minneapolis-St. Paul
full_article:
Nepal flooding kills 1,300, hundreds still missing Ten days after flooding in Nepal that has left 1,300 people dead, rescuers were able to pull two men from the rubble. The rescue is offering hope that others might still be found alive as hundreds are believed to still be trapped underneath the devastation. FOX's Stephanie Bennett has more.

The Brief A doctor who recently completed a fellowship at the University of Minnesota and three family members, including his wife who was a former psychiatrist at Mercy Hospital – Unity Campus, were reported missing Tuesday after catastrophic flooding in Nepal. More than 1,300 people died after a glacier collapse near the Nepal-China border triggered massive flooding on Aug. 26. Recovery efforts are ongoing, and Nepal observed a national day of mourning Monday.



(FOX 9) - A University of Minnesota doctor and his family, including his wife who was a former psychiatrist at Mercy Hospital – Unity Campus in Fridley, have been declared missing after devastating floods swept through Nepal on August 26.

U of M doctor missing in Nepal

What we know:

Ishan Patel, a doctor who recently completed a fellowship at the U of M, and three of his family members were reported missing on Tuesday after catastrophic flooding struck Nepal.

The university shared on social media that Patel, a recent graduate of its Adult Reconstructive Fellowship, had traveled to Nepal with his wife, Akanksha Patel, his mother, Shilpa Patel, and his father-in-law, Umesh Kumar.

According to university officials, the group was on a pilgrimage following his graduation when the flooding occurred.

Patel and his family were likely at their hotel when the floodwaters hit. The hotel was swept away by the surge, the university says.

What they're saying:

"Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with Dr. Patel, his family, and all those affected by this tragedy," the post by university officials said in part.

Allina Health has provided FOX 9 with the following statement: "We are deeply saddened to hear reports involving Dr. Akanksha Patel and the tragedy in Nepal. Dr. Patel was not a current employee but previously worked as a psychiatrist at Mercy Hospital – Unity Campus. Our thoughts are with her family, friends and all those affected during this difficult time."

The backstory:

The flooding followed a glacier collapse near the Nepal-China border on Aug. 26, triggering a massive torrent of water and mud that devastated mountain communities.

More than 1,300 people have so far been declared dead as a result.

Nepal observed a national day of mourning Monday, according to the country's disaster management agency.

What we don't know:

Rescuers are still actively searching for survivors, and the situation continues to evolve.

It is not yet known whether Patel and his family members have been located.

The Source: Information provided by a University of Minnesota social media post, Nepal's disaster management agency and previous FOX 9 reporting.

title: Roma to wear jersey supporting Nepal in Champions League match - Arab News
description: Roma to wear jersey supporting Nepal in Champions League match  Arab News
publisher.title: Arab News
full_article:
ROME: Roma said Wednesday they will play this week’s Champions League match against Fenerbahce in jerseys supporting the relief effort in Nepal, after being banned from displaying their usual sponsor in Turkiye.

A flash flood on August 26 caused by a glacier and rockslide, which began on the China-Nepal border, has left at least 1,410 people dead and 5,651 missing.

“The visitors will take to the pitch with the World Food Programme (WFP) logo on the front of their shirts,” the Italian club said ahead of Thursday’s game in Istanbul.

Roma’s usual shirt sponsor is a sports betting company which is banned from advertising under Turkish law.

The one-off jersey bearing the logo of the WFP, a Rome-based agency of the United Nations, will also feature the message “Together for Nepal”.

“The shirts worn by Gian Piero Gasperini’s players during the match will be auctioned, with all funds raised going toward supporting the people of Nepal through the WFP’s relief efforts,” Roma added.

title: 2 doctors with Minnesota ties declared missing in Nepal floods - 5 EYEWITNESS NEWS
description: 2 doctors with Minnesota ties declared missing in Nepal floods  5 EYEWITNESS NEWS
publisher.title: 5 EYEWITNESS NEWS
full_article:
Two doctors with Minnesota ties and family members were declared missing on Tuesday after catastrophic flooding in Nepal two weeks ago.

In a social media post, the University of Minnesota Department of Orthopedic Surgery said Dr. Ishan Patel traveled to Nepal on a pilgrimage after graduating from its Adult Reconstructive Fellowship. He was accompanied by his wife, Dr. Akanksha Patel; his mother, Shilpa Patel; and his father-in-law, Umesh Kumar.

Dr. Akanksha Patel previously worked at Mercy Hospital as a psychiatrist, a spokesperson for Allina Health told 5 EYEWITNESS NEWS.

According to the university department, available information indicated the family was staying at a hotel when flooding struck the region. Floodwaters swept away the hotel and all four were declared missing.

An Allina Health spokesperson said, “We are deeply saddened to hear reports involving Dr. Akanksha Patel and the tragedy in Nepal. Dr. Patel was not a current employee but previously worked as a psychiatrist at Mercy Hospital – Unity Campus. Our thoughts are with her family, friends and all those affected during this difficult time.”

The flooding followed a glacier collapse near the Nepal-China border on Aug. 26, triggering a massive torrent of water and mud that devastated mountain communities.

On Monday, the Associated Press reported more than 1,300 people died in Nepal and Tibet, and about 5,000 others remained missing, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency. Nepal observed a national day of mourning on Monday.

“This situation continues to evolve, and recovery efforts in the region are ongoing,” the university department said. “Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with Dr. Patel, his family, and all those affected by this tragedy.”

title: Nepal seeks survivors two weeks after deadly floods - Courthouse News
description: Nepal seeks survivors two weeks after deadly floods  Courthouse News
publisher.title: Courthouse News
full_article:
(AFP) — Nepali rescuers clung to hopes of finding survivors trapped in hydropower tunnels Wednesday, two weeks after deadly flooding triggered by a glacial mountain collapse.

The Aug. 26 tsunami-like surge of water, mud and debris, which began along the China-Nepal border, has killed more than 1,410 people and left 5,651 missing.

“The search-and-rescue operation in the tunnels at the Trishuli 3A, Trishuli 3B and Chilime hydropower projects is ongoing,” Nepal Army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet told AFP.

In Nepal, 1,367 bodies have been recovered and 5,132 people remain missing, the country’s disaster authority said Wednesday.

In China, 43 people are dead and 519 are missing, according to state media.

Hundreds of foreigners and hydropower workers are among the missing.

Three people have been rescued from deep inside the tunnels — two Nepalis on Friday and a Chinese man on Saturday.

But there has been no official confirmation of additional survivors since then.

Thousands of people displaced by the disaster are living in camps, and the charity Save the Children said as many as 540 children had been separated from their parents.

Nepal police said they were taking extra precautions to protect children and women in relief camps.

“We have become more vigilant in temporary holding centres in the affected areas where there are children, women or minority groups who could be victims of sexual abuse,” Nepal Police spokesman Abi Narayan Kafle said.

“We have also started providing psychosocial counselling in different camps,” he told AFP.

Although the exact cause of the glacial collapse is unclear, climate change is accelerating glacial melt worldwide and increasing the risk of such disasters.

Nepal, a largely rural nation of 30 million people that has contributed little to the greenhouse gas emissions driving global warming, has said reconstruction could cost billions of dollars.

Kafle said security personnel had enlisted community members to search for people feared buried under debris.

“We have started a special search campaign for missing bodies all across the Bhotekoshi river corridor,” he said.

“We are also using drones to search for bodies.”

title: Nepal’s high-altitude wildernesses & wildlife are increasingly under threat (commentary) - news - Mongabay
description: Nepal’s high-altitude wildernesses & wildlife are increasingly under threat (commentary)  news - Mongabay

full_article:
High-altitude wildernesses like Limi Valley in Nepal are suffering from human encroachment, which is advancing at an unprecedented pace, pushing wildlife into ever-smaller pockets of shrinking habitat.

Creatures ranging from wild yaks to Himalayan wolves, snow leopards, Eurasian lynx, Tibetan brown bears and Pallas’s cats are under pressure from a new wave of herders bringing sheep, goats and dogs into the remotest areas, spreading disease and degrading grazing lands.

“What this high-altitude landscape, its people, and biodiversity need is straightforward: formal legal ecosystem protection from the Nepalese government, led by the stewardship of the Limi community who are best placed to protect it, and supported by conservation organizations,” a new op-ed argues.

This article is a commentary. The views expressed are those of the authors, not necessarily of Mongabay. See All Key Ideas

Changes like increasing geological and glacial instability driven by the warming climate are a growing concern across the Himalayas. Our hearts go out to the thousands of families across Nepal, China, and around the world grieving their loved ones and searching for those missing after the recent catastrophic flash flood at the Nepal-China border.

Though nearly 400 kilometers (almost 250 miles) to the northwest of the recent flash flood zone, our study area in Nepal’s Limi Valley in Upper Humla — a landscape with several villages and a rich wildlife heritage, that we have spent years trying to understand and protect — is also affected by such changes.

Limi Valley has been wild for as long as we’ve studied it, but not anymore.

After many days of travel to reach the study area recently, our team was excited to check on the Himalayan wolves, to see if its family would be denning in the same spot as last year. We found no wolves. Instead, we found thousands of sheep and goats, trailed by herders from lower-lying villages, free-ranging herd dogs, and patches of burning vegetation.

A Himalayan wolf in its natural habitat in Limi Valley, northwestern Nepal. Photo courtesy of Himalayan Wolves Project.

Every season we return, there is less wild left to find.

Upper Humla’s once-pristine high-altitude habitats are suffering from human encroachment advancing at an unprecedented pace, pushing wildlife into ever-smaller pockets of shrinking habitat. While formal protection of this unique ecosystem has been on the political agenda for many years, it can’t wait much longer.

Transformed landscape

Upper Humla presents an important high-altitude refuge for wildlife. At its northern edge, Limi Valley forms a transboundary ecosystem corridor connecting Nepal to the Tibetan Plateau. Over the past decade, researchers have documented a wealth of charismatic and globally threatened wildlife in the area such as wild yak ( Bos mutus ) — a rediscovery for Nepal — the Himalayan wolf ( Canis lupus chanco ), snow leopard ( Panthera uncia ), Eurasian lynx ( Lynx lynx ), Tibetan brown bear ( Ursus arctos pruinosus ), Pallas’s cat ( Otocolobus manul ), steppe polecat ( Mustela eversmanii ), the country’s largest population of kiang ( Equus kiang ) — the world’s largest wild ass — Himalayan marmot ( Marmota himalayana ), mountain weasel ( Mustela altaica ), various species of pikas ( Ochotona spp.), as well as an outstanding diversity of birds and plants.

This biological richness is now disappearing fast.

In just a few years, Limi Valley has seen a drastic increase in domestic sheep and goats brought in from outside the valley to graze its high-altitude rangelands. This year, we found at least eight to 10 sheep- and goat-herding camps in the upper valleys beyond Pulgaon Pass (i.e., Sakya, Gyau, Chyakpolung, and Mergyu Khola), with roughly 400-500 animals and three to six herding dogs per camp. Dozens more camps were scattered across the lower Limi landscape around Takche and Talun Khola, adding up to many thousands of sheep and goats and hundreds of free-ranging dogs suddenly in the wildlife’s habitat.

A sheep and goat herding camp with four herd dogs assembles for the night in Chyakpolung, Upper Limi, Humla, Nepal. Image courtesy of Geraldine Werhahn / Himalayan Wolves Project.

Just a few years ago, traditional herding of yak and jhoppa (a yak-cow hybrid) by the local people of Limi was the norm here, but not anymore. The shift from this to large-scale sheep and goat herding brings new problems that this fragile high-altitude ecosystem has not faced before, like the following.

Overgrazing and disease risk

Thousands of sheep and goats graze intensively on all types of herbs, shrubs, and grass shoots, damaging the fragile high-altitude flora far more severely than traditional yak herding, which is typically lower-density and locally regulated. They also act as potential sources of diseases, such as sheep and goat plague, a highly contagious viral disease that can infect domestic and wild ruminants sharing the same pastures. In a remote landscape with almost no veterinary services or wildlife health monitoring, an outbreak could spread widely before it’s even detected.

Dogs on the loose

Well-trained and closely supervised dogs can help herders protect livestock from predators, but most of the dogs we observed were unsupervised, underfed, and roaming as far as 10 kilometers (6 miles) from camps to hunt marmots, woolly hares and pikas, and hound wild ungulates in the last untouched corners where wildlife generally retreats.

We witnessed the consequences directly, like when a pack of roaming dogs encroached on an active wolf den in one of those remote upper valleys, forcing the pack to fight off the dogs just 500 meters (just over a quarter of a mile) from their two young pups. Disturbance at a den during pup-rearing is one of the most consequential disruptions a wolf pack can experience, and such physical encounters also pose the risk of disease transmission.

Herding dogs resting by a livestock camp in Upper Limi, Humla Nepal. Well-trained and closely supervised dogs can help herders protect livestock from predators, but most dogs observed in Upper Humla were unsupervised, underfed, and roaming as far as 10 kilometers from camps, hunting and harassing wildlife. Image courtesy of Geraldine Werhahn / Himalayan Wolves Project.

By contrast, traditional yak herding by Limi people involves no dogs, and the large-bodied yaks and jhoppas are rarely susceptible to predation, except for their calves, which receive special protection from the local herders.

Fewer wild prey and growing conflict

Compared to high-altitude-adapted yaks and jhoppas, sheep and goats are much more vulnerable to predation due to their small size. As livestock numbers rise in wild habitats, so does the conflict, and in return, retaliatory killing of wolves and other carnivores preying on sheep or goats that compete with large herbivores such as wild yak, kiang, Tibetan gazelle, argali, and blue sheep for grazing grounds, while also disturbing smaller species such as Himalayan marmots and pikas.

These wild herbivores form the natural prey base that carnivores depend on, so expanding livestock numbers mean wild prey populations are left with fewer resources. As wild prey populations decline, carnivores inevitably turn to livestock, escalating the human-wildlife conflict.

Eroding stewardship in a changing climate

The sheep and goat herders arriving in Limi come from lower-lying villages with no connection to this landscape, and they often lack the sense of stewardship that the local community holds for its land and wildlife. Unlike yak herders, who traditionally use dried yak dung as cooking fuel, these visiting herders cut the valley’s scarce high-altitude shrubs for firewood, adding pressure to an already fragile rangeland. In addition, some of these herders are also involved in illegal wildlife killing and trade of wildlife body parts.

A recently built road cutting through core wildlife habitat in Gyau, Upper Limi, Humla, Nepal, one of the last refuges in the region for kiang, wild yaks and Himalayan wolves. The road was built hoping to attract more religious tourism and is not of general use to the local community, but it has become a route for the illegal wildlife trade across the border. Image courtesy of Geraldine Werhahn / Himalayan Wolves Project.

For generations, Limi Valley has been sustained by its people and their timeless traditions guiding sustainable stewardship of the land. Its three villages — Til, Halji, and Dzang — have been inhabited for centuries, with Til believed to have been settled for at least 1,000 years. Similarly, Limi’s people have managed their natural resources through traditional management systems that intertwine ecology, culture, religion, and livelihood, keeping nature and people in balance.

That balance is now being eroded.

Limi is at a turning point, both for its natural wealth and traditional culture, as it gradually loses the very people who have safeguarded these landscapes generation after generation. Opportunities in cities, along with increasingly difficult living conditions in the valley, are pushing families away, leaving outsiders with no lasting stake in its future.

Glacial lake outburst floods have already destroyed local bridges more than once this year in Limi, forcing families to relocate with little support or warning. These events may be smaller in scale than what we just witnessed, but they offer a sobering glimpse of the cascading high-mountain hazards that, on Aug. 26, swept through the Bhote Koshi-Trishuli corridor of central Nepal, leaving behind a scale of loss and devastation difficult to measure and comprehend.

A small herd of kiang in Upper Limi, Humla Nepal. The species has been declining drastically over the past decade due to intensifying human habitat encroachment. Image courtesy of Geraldine Werhahn / Himalayan Wolves Project.

Running out of time

Wildlife in Limi has shown resilience, but time is clearly running out now.

The kiang population has declined sharply over the past decade, and this year, our focal wolf pack had just two pups, the lowest reproductive success we have recorded in a decade of monitoring. Reproduction varies naturally, and while one year does not define a trend, in a landscape under such rapid disturbance, these warning signals can’t be ignored.

Carnivores like wolves and snow leopards face mounting threats, too, like retaliatory killing after livestock losses, poaching linked to illegal wildlife trade across the Nepal-Tibet border, and the ever-lurking threat of poison, which kills even the most resilient carnivores, along with nontarget scavengers that feed on the same carcass. Poison is used illegally to kill carnivores worldwide, including across the Indian subcontinent and the Himalayas.

Transboundary corridors like Limi and its wildernesses are quietly disappearing under a similar combination of pressures: retreating traditional livelihoods, expanding commercial herding, weak governance in remote borderlands, lack of law enforcement, and a changing climate that is destabilizing glaciers and water sources.

A young Pallas’s cat. Image courtesy of Sebastian Kennerknecht/Cat Expeditions.

Formal ecosystem protection needed

What this high-altitude landscape, its people, and biodiversity need is straightforward: formal legal ecosystem protection from the Nepalese government, led by the stewardship of the Limi community who are best placed to protect it, and supported by conservation organizations. Protection, however, should not come at the expense of local livelihoods. Dedicated, sustainably managed pasturelands could provide secure grazing areas for herders while keeping large, critical wildlife habitats relatively undisturbed.

Upper Limi is an extraordinary refuge of Himalayan biodiversity in Nepal and beyond. It is not worth losing this unique high-altitude ecosystem and its charismatic species of plants and animals to uncontrolled livestock herding. It needs safeguarding before its natural wealth is irreversibly diminished.

The last patches of intact nature on this planet are disappearing fast. Upper Limi is one of the last.

Let’s protect it.

Geraldine Werhahn is co-chair of the IUCN SSC Canid Specialist Group and director of the Himalayan Wolves Project. Sabita Gurung is a project officer at the Himalayan Wolves Project.

title: Recent University of Minnesota medical fellowship graduate, family missing after Nepal flooding - MPR News
description: Recent University of Minnesota medical fellowship graduate, family missing after Nepal flooding  MPR News
publisher.title: MPR News
full_article:
The University of Minnesota says a recent graduate of one of its medical fellowship programs is among the thousands of people missing after last month’s flash flooding in Nepal and Tibet.

The university’s Department of Orthopedic Surgery said Tuesday that Dr. Ishan Patel and his wife, Akanksha Patel, were on a pilgrimage after he graduated from the adult reconstructive surgery fellowship.

The U said they were joined by his mother, Shilpa Patel, and his father-in-law, Umeshkumar Patel, when the flooding occurred on Aug. 26.

“According to available information, Dr. Patel and his family were likely at their hotel when catastrophic flooding occurred. The hotel was swept away by the floodwaters, and Dr. Patel and his family are currently declared missing,” the university reported.

Houses damaged by flash floods are seen on the bank of Trishuli River in Dhunge in the Nuwakot District of Nepal on Monday. Niranjan Shrestha | AP

“This situation continues to evolve, and recovery efforts in the region are ongoing. Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with Dr. Patel, his family, and all those affected by this tragedy,” the university’s statement said.

The Patels are dual U.S.-Canadian citizens, and their parents are from Canada. Relatives told the CBC that the long-planned pilgrimage was to mark the start of Dr. Patel’s new career — and that family members have traveled to Nepal to help search for their loved ones.

The Associated Press reported earlier this week that the flooding killed more than 1,300 people — with about 5,000 still unaccounted for. Nepal observed a day of mourning on Monday, as search efforts continue.
